title: Production possibility frontier
examples: What does the shape of the PPF tell us about an economy?
If the economy moves outside the PPF, what does that mean?
How does technological advancement affect the PPF?

explain.say: Today we are looking at the production possibility frontier. This curve shows maximum output possible.
Being efficient means producing at the curve itself. This uses all available resources fully.
If we produce inside the curve, we are inefficient. We are not using all our resources well.
When the curve shifts outwards, it shows economic growth. More is possible overall.
An everyday example is a local bakery. Better ovens mean they can bake more bread and cakes.

draw.text: Real life: Better ovens = more output

explain.say: A common mistake is thinking all shifts are due to resources. Technology is also a major cause.

faq.q: What does the curve itself represent?
faq.a: The curve shows the maximum combination of two goods an economy can produce with its current resources and technology.
asks: What is the limit of production?

faq.q: If the curve shifts out, what is happening in the economy?
faq.a: It means the economy has grown because it can now produce more of both goods than before.
asks: How do we get more output?
What causes the PPF to expand?

faq.q: What does it mean to be inefficient?
faq.a: It means the economy is wasting resources or labour and is not producing the maximum possible amount of goods.
asks: What if we are inside the curve?
Is it bad to be inside the curve?

faq.a: Yes, it can shift in if resources are destroyed, like by a natural disaster or war.
asks: Can the economy shrink its potential?

faq.q: Does the shape of the curve matter?
faq.a: The shape shows opportunity cost. Concave shapes show increasing opportunity cost.
asks: What does the shape tell us about trade-offs?

facts: The PPF illustrates the trade-offs between producing two goods.
Points on the curve represent efficient production.
An outward shift indicates economic growth or improvement.
A shift inward suggests a decrease in available resources.

quiz.say: If an economy can produce 10 units of apples or 20 units of oranges, what is the opportunity cost of 10 apples?
quiz.why: The trade-off shows that giving up 20 oranges allows for 10 apples.

wrong.1: This confuses the amount of apples with the amount of oranges given up.
wrong.2: This only states the amount of apples without considering the trade-off.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes that producing apples costs nothing in terms of oranges.

quiz.say: If the PPF shifts outwards, what is the most likely cause?
quiz.why: New technology allows the economy to produce more output overall.

wrong.0: Fewer workers would cause the curve to shift inwards, not outwards.
wrong.1: Destruction of resources causes a reduction in potential, shifting the curve inwards.
wrong.2: Unemployment means resources are unused, which is a point inside the curve, not a shift.

quiz.say: Which situation represents an inefficient use of resources?

options.show: A factory running at half capacity
options.say: A factory running at half capacity

quiz.why: Running below maximum capacity means resources are underused, placing the point inside the frontier.

wrong.1: A point on the curve represents full and efficient use of all resources.
wrong.2: A shift outwards represents a change in potential, not the current level of output.
wrong.3: A point outside the curve is currently impossible to achieve with existing resources.
